subtopic: B.C. SALMON-REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS WITH U.S.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. J. Robichaud (Minister of Fisheries):
subtopic: B.C. SALMON-REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS WITH U.S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the salmon discussions in Seattle concluded yesterday, I wish to make a brief statement in order to inform the house as to the results of the deliberations.
While some progress has been made in the discussions in Seattle in recent days through clarification of points at issue, I regret to say that we have not, in our opinion, moved substantially toward an acceptable solution of our problem. Canada has always believed the seaward net fishing limits should be used as a tool to minimize the catching by one country of salmon bound for the rivers of the other. It is to that end that we have presented at meetings held in Washington last fall, in Ottawa in February and in the last three days at Seattle proposals for the inward adjustment of the limits both in Alaska and in British Columbia.
We were prepared to accept further curtailment of Canadian fisheries in the interests of better management and of equity. We believe that the over-all effect of the Canadian proposal made at these meetings would be advantageous to both countries through better management resulting from Canada and the United States each harvesting their own stocks separately.
The new line we proposed for the Alaska area was comparable to the line established along the B.C. coast in 1957. As the United States representatives have refused to accept our proposal, we have no alternative but to state that we reserve the right to extend Canadian fisheries seaward where appropriate to correct the inequitable situation which exists under present conditions. It is with regret that we feel compelled to take such a position, as we would have preferred the course we have presented, that is the inward adjustment of seaward fishing limits to minimize the interception by one country of salmon bound for the other. We still believe that in the long run such an adjustment would have been beneficial to both countries.
I must add, however, that we have agreed at this meeting to initiate a research program designed to give more information on the
May 20. 1966

Salmon Fishery Negotiations movements and intermingling of the stock harvested in Alaskan and Canadian rivers. Such research, we hope, will assist in arriving in the future at solutions to the problems now arising from interception by one country of salmon bound to the other. While we recognize that the problems we have been discussing were complex and difficult, we still believe that discussions must be resumed in the near future on broader aspects of the subjects we have been raising at these particular meetings.
At the same time I wish to make clear that the Canadian government has no intention of authorizing salmon net fishing on the high seas.

subtopic: B.C. SALMON-REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS WITH U.S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the minister for giving us in advance a copy of the statement he has just made. We are not surprised by the attitude taken by the United States government in view of their lack of co-operation at the meetings last fall in Washington, and in view of a public statement made by a certain powerful U.S. senator.
Just last week the fisheries committee passed a resolution which we hoped would strengthen the hand of the Canadian negotiators. It is very discouraging to note the attitude taken toward the principle that the country where the salmon originate has a certain right to them. If the United States will not grant this right to us, what inducement will there be to the Canadian people to continue the rehabilitation of our own species?
I am encouraged by the minister's statement that the Canadian government reserves the right to extend Canadian fisheries seaward where considered advisable. I hope these are not mere words. For many years the United States government has threatened to retaliate, in the event of such a step, by closing our market for fish in the United States. This is a specious argument, because there is a world shortage of fish. If the United States were to cut off our imports they would be cutting off their nose to spite their face. I hope the Canadian government will show courage in this respect.
I am pleased there is to be further research with regard to the origin of the salmon. I notice that the minister did not say the Americans denied they were catching our salmon. There is ample proof that they are. Whether further research will do anything more to convince them, I cannot say. I hope 
the Canadian government will take a firm and bold stand on this matter. The people of Canada and of British Columbia will demand it.

subtopic: B.C. SALMON-REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS WITH U.S.
speechtext:
We regret that the minister should have been forced into the position of having to make a statement such as the one to which the house has just listened. The United States has a history of destroying natural resources in the process of their exploiting. They destroyed the salmon runs on the Columbia river by building dams all over the place, and now they are seeking to exploit and destroy salmon runs in Canadian territory by the use of fish traps. Wanton destruction of Alaskan salmon runs was carried out by the United States, and now they seek to do the same sort of thing here by refusing to negotiate as far as home-bound Canadian salmon are concerned.
It is indicative of their attitude that a two-faced policy is followed in this respect on the part of the United States authorities. On the one hand the Alaska government has spoken most belligerently to the Japanese fishermen, ordering them to keep out of the Bristol bay area and cease fishing for what they call red salmon homebound for Alaskan waters, on the ground that prior right rests with the United States. On the other hand an entirely different view is taken in discussions with Canada when the same principle is involved. There has been concern about the surf line or net fishing limit ever since 1957, when the United States refused to carry out the principle of an understanding which had been reached at that time and extended its net salmon fishing limits three miles outward into the ocean while we kept ours close to shore.
There is unanimity of opinion in Canada in the fishing industry, in the unions, in government circles, certainly in parliament and in the fisheries committee upon this question. The feeling is unanimous that the United States surf line in Alaskan waters should be drawn in so as to ensure that American fishermen are not catching and exploiting our homebound salmon. This has been happening to such an extent that in some Alaskan waters between 60 and 70 per cent of the total catch consists of Canadian salmon coming home to spawn. Exploitation of this sort can lead to nothing less than the destruction of the resource.
We very much regret that the discussions in Seattle have broken down. I do not think we can dignify what took place by the name
May 20, 1966

"negotiations" because it is obvious that the United States government did not want to negotiate anything, as is indicated by its arrogant and domineering attitude at these meetings and its refusal to modify this position.
[DOT] (11:20 a.m.)
This leaves us with no alternative, I submit, but to carry out the earlier pronouncements of the Canadian government, which means there is no agreement about net fishing limits. Consequently we have to either eliminate those limits or move them seaward so Canadian fishermen can engage in the same sort of practice, regrettable as it might be, to give our fishermen the opportunity to catch as many of these United States or Alaskan bound salmon as they can. Perhaps this sort of regrettable action will force the United States into a reasonable position, where they will sit down to discuss and negotiate this particular question fairly.
May I say one more word. If we are going to engage in additional research, I suggest to the minister that he use the services of the Canadian navy in conducting that research.

subtopic: B.C. SALMON-REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS WITH U.S.
speechtext:
In the absence of the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson), who is on the committee, I should like to say that we also regret very much that the minister, who is very conscientious and hard working in this business of preserving the fishing industry, had to make this particular statement. I have reason to say this, because I have had problems in connection with fishing and lumbering in my constituency, and I must say that the co-operation I have had from the minister has been very good indeed.
Many salmon have their birth place in the Cariboo constituency, as in Skeena. We realize that a great deal of work is being done in this particular area by the Canadian fisheries department to preserve these fish. Unfortunately it seems that we are not getting a fair deal in connection with the catching of the fish we are raising in Canada. I hope the minister will be able to carry out the program he has suggested, and that we will be able to negotiate with the United States to get a working arrangement under which the maximum amount of fish can be produced in British Columbia and caught by our own fishermen.

1. Postal services including Canada's share of the upkeep of the international bureaux at Berne and Montevideo, $252,804,000.

Mr. Chairman, when we
reached the termination of the discussion of the estimates of the department last night I was on my feet addressing a few remarks to the Postmaster General in connection with this years' estimates and the policies of his department. In spite of the fact that I have always found the present Postmaster General a very co-operative member of the government in respect of problems I have raised with him, I could not see my way clear to accept his suggestion that the matter I want to raise be dealt with between us in his office.
I have had a rather lengthy correspondence with the minister, extending from some time last December until March of this year, as a result of which I feel that this is a matter which can only be pursued further by airing it in public on the floor of this house. Were it not for that fact I might have been inclined to agree to his suggestion and not refer to this matter at this time.
There is one other matter which I intended to raise, but in my desire to co-operate with the hon. member for Ontario I shall refrain

May 20, 1966
Supply-Post Office
from doing so, except to say that it is a hardy perennial type of problem. I have discussed this on many occasions with postmasters general, and if the present minister cares to look back at past years' considerations of these estimates he will find that I have been concerned about the fact that while we have been boasting that we were the first in the world to establish an all-up mail service for faster delivery by air, this policy has been somewhat restricted by its application to main fine carriers. Arrangements have apparently still not been worked out to make possible air distribution of mail to many smaller communities where lines are running. As I have pointed out, in one particular case mail that could be delivered in ten minutes by plane requires three weeks for delivery and the return reply.
The particular matter I should like to raise at this time arises from a situation which I have been wrestling with most of the time since I became a member of this house.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
It is a situation in which a great many Canadians find themselves because of the nature of our country and the type of industrial development taking place. As a result many people are robbed of what I consider to be their basic right to public delivery of mail by the post office. I am referring to those who are required in the course of earning their living to go to places where living facilities are provided entirely by private companies.
I have had an exchange of correspondence with the minister on this topic in recent months with respect to one particular place. Perhaps I might refer to a letter which the minister addressed to me on January 13 of this year in which he said in part:
I should like to stress that the establishment of post offices in company towns such as Benson Lake where the town is under the complete jurisdiction of the company is dependent on the willingness of the company to provide the necessary accommodation for postal purposes and the necessary staff to operate a post office.
The minister went on to explain that the Post Office Department does not directly operate the post offices in smaller communities but that the postmasters are responsible for the provision of accommodation.
In this particular case we would certainly consider the appointment of someone other than the company if they were able to meet the requirements. However, inquiries and discussions with representatives of the company reveal that no one was willing to assume charge of a post office at that point.

I replied to that letter and expressed my disagreement with the position being taken by the Postmaster General. In a letter to the minister dated February 28 I said in part:
I must reiterate my position that Canadian law should be such that official jurisdiction of the post office should extend to the point of delivery to individual Canadians wherever residential quarters of any permanence are established even though these may be owned and operated by a single private firm.
In reply I had a letter from the minister dated March 21 in which he said:
I have noted your remark that Canadian law should be such that official jurisdiction of the Post Office Department should extend to the point of delivery to individual Canadian citizens wherever residential quarters of any permanence are established.
In this regard I should like to quote Part 2 (b) of the Post Office Act-
The reference is to the section which defines "delivery". So far as I am concerned the minister missed the whole point I was making. He gave no indication whether he or the government would be prepared to consider making a change in the existing law, and while I thank the minister for drawing my attention to that particular section of the legislation I would point out that the Post Office Act is a public document a copy of which I have in my office. His reply of March 21 is certainly no answer to the question I had in mind, whether he or the government would consider correcting what I believe to be a basic injustice to individual Canadian citizens.
I do not intend to take the time of the committee by giving detailed examples of the kind of abuses of the right of individuals to receipt of mail which have occurred to my own knowledge. In this parliament, however, there appears to be an increasing and welcome concern about the rights and freedoms of Canadian citizens. I am not talking about survey crews of half a dozen men who move across the country, camp in tents and do not stay in one spot for longer than two or three days. I am contending that if there is a permanent logging or mining camp where living quarters are provided by the employer, Canadian law should be framed in such a way that it would no longer be up to the operators of the residential community concerned to decide at their own sweet pleasure whether they should enable those living in that community to have the benefit of a proper postal service. This is the issue and I feel we should have an answer from the hon. gentleman on this question.
May 20, 1966

I can refer to one section of the Post Office Act which the minister did not mention in his letter, section 8, where it is stated that the postmaster shall have the sole and exclusive privilege of collecting, conveying and delivering letters within Canada. I would argue that this should not only be his exclusive privilege but also his exclusive responsibility. I shall not enter now upon a discussion of what one hon. member some years ago called the bootlegging of mail in Canada but I am concerned, as I say, with the abuses which have been taking place in this area involving the right of Canadians to have their mail safely delivered.
I will give just one example. A number of years ago arrangements were made for the delivery of certain parcels to workers in areas where there were no liquor vending stores. The normal arrangement was to carry in the mail from the post office to the community concerned. But the whole arrangement was invalidated when the company concerned refused to carry this particular type of mail to the men living in the community, a logging camp.
Cut off the booze.

I said at the time that should an individual employee abuse his right recourse was available to the company but that it was improper and contrary to our concept of justice that any private organization should be able to deny to a citizen his normal right to receive mail addressed to him.
Or to interfere with Her Majesty's mail.

I am not sure whether legally or technically the company could be considered as having done that. The company told its employees: If you want to go 60 miles down the logging railroad to the post office, you can pick it up yourselves. But the men were entirely dependent on company transport in any case. I presented the argument but could not get agreement from the government at the time that there was technically any interference with the mail.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
At this point I should like to remind the Postmaster General of the discussion we had in this house the other day led by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources who painted a glowing picture of the possibilities for the future development of the far north. He described in some detail the resource possibilities of that area. I suggest to 23033-340
Supply-Post Office
the Postmaster General that if this kind of development is going to take place much of it will come about through the establishment of the type of communities about which I am concerned.
This problem is not confined to one particular constituency or area of Canada but is one which will be of concern to members in every quarter of this house. If the present Post Office Act does not allow the Postmaster General, in the kind of situation I am describing where people are residing, to require a post office to be established and someone to operate it under his jurisdiction, then the act should be changed. Appropriate legislation should be introduced without further delay to rectify what in my view is a very longstanding problem and legitimate grievance on the part of many Canadians who go forth to do the hard work of producing the wealth which enables us to enjoy the standard of living that we have been able to achieve.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to delay the passage of these estimates but there are matters which I feel I should bring to the attention of the minister. I congratulate him upon his appointment to the portfolio of Postmaster General. Although I have quite a number of new post offices in my constituency, there is a need for more. The areas that need post offices are mostly areas in which private homes or buildings are rented by the Post Office Department and the service provided by these offices is not of the type the people would like. Under these circumstances we cannot blame the operators of these offices for not giving the service the people would like to have. It is for this reason I should like to see more new post offices erected in my area.
Another complaint I have received concerns the mail truck contractors. They are faced with increased expenses compared with the time when they entered into their contracts. The price of trucks is higher than it was then and operating expenses have increased as well. I believe these contracts should be reviewed more often than they are now. Many people who entered into these contracts could be earning better wages if they had accepted other types of employment. I emphasize the point strongly that these contracts should be reviewed more often and consideration should be given to the fact that the cost of living as well as the cost of their equipment is going up.
There is one more matter I should like to bring to the attention of the Postmaster

May 20, 1966
Supply-Post Office
General. I refer to the fact that the telephones have been removed from some of the larger post offices. This causes hardship not only for the post office officials but for the people living in the country, particularly in the wintertime when it is often difficult to get to town. The telephones which have been removed should be reinstalled and telephones should be installed in those places which have not had them.
These are the essential matters I should like to bring to the attention of the Postmaster General. As I said at the outset, I cannot complain too much about the department's lack of consideration of the need for post offices in my area. There may be other areas with priority. However, I believe there should be new post offices erected to replace the buildings that have been rented in order to provide service for the people.

Mr. Chairman, I intend to speak for only a minute or two. I should like to raise two problems with the Postmaster General. I may say that to date I am batting .667 with him and I hope I will finish the session that way. One of the problems concerning post offices in my area involves the Department of Public Works. I understand this department is building the small post offices in that area. I would ask the minister to advise the post office officials not to take over these new buildings until they are completed. The fact is that the Post Office Department has rushed into the new building before the general contractor has completed his job; possibly some of the mechanical trades have not completed their work. Once the department occupies the new building the subcontractors or the suppliers of subcontractors are often faced with having to wait six to eight months and in some cases up to a year before being paid by the contractor. I think we could avoid this situation and help these people by not accepting post offices until they are formally taken over by the Department of Public Works. In one case I know that an amount of $12,000 is owing to a supplier by the subcontractor who has been paid a fair amount of his money. However, he is not in a rush to complete the job and this has put the supplier in an awkward position.
The other problem I should like to raise with the minister relates to the small mail contract amounting to $800 or $900. Some of these contracts were made before changes were made by Canadian National which transports the mail in the first place. About 60 per

cent of the time the trains are late, and I do not mean by 10 or 15 minutes but two or three hours late. These contract mail carriers now have to spend the major part of the day waiting at the railway station for the train to arrive. They are losing other income by so doing. I have written to the minister concerning the problem and this is the third of my batting average where I have not been successful. I ask him again to reconsider these cases so these people will receive consideration for the time spent waiting for trains.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to talk more than 30 minutes on the estimates of the Post Office Department.
I would like to say how much I appreciate the co-operation I have received so far from the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote). He has been friendly, conciliating and he has accepted several of the suggestions made to him. I thank him very sincerely.
However, and quite rightly, that does not prevent us from having our little problems, because quite often the settlement of a problem creates new ones. Consequently, one must not be surprised to see problems arise in various ridings.
Last year, I made strong representations to the minister about the post office in Rouyn. I understand that the matter concerns mostly the Department of Public Works, but the Post Office Department is also concerned, because I am sure that if the Postmaster General requested the building of a new post office in Rouyn, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcllraith) would not take long to accede to his request.
As I have said already, I am wondering what architect is responsible for the eyesore we have in Rouyn. I secured pictures of it, which I showed the minister, and I feel that one must be blind not to see how dreadful such a building is, when there are such nice post offices in Noranda, Malartic, Cadillac and Val d'Or.
And yet, the city of Rouyn, the metropolis of the northwest of the province, has a post office which, as we say so well in French, is not fit to be looked at.
It is probably not an architect who prepared the plans, but an official of the Public Works Department who tried to play a trick on the Postmaster General by giving us such a building. In any case, once again I call the minister's attention to that matter.
May 20, 1966

There is another thing I want to point out to him. It is the postal service in Val d'Or.
Last week, while I was in Val d'Or, I met the municipal authorities who told me about the slowness of the letter delivery service from Montreal or Ottawa. It seems that it takes two, three and even four days for letters to reach Val d'Or. There is undoubtedly something wrong with mail transportation or letter delivery.
I know that departmental officials will examine my remarks, and there is surely room for improvement within the department. As a matter of fact, there is no reason why the mail from Montreal or Ottawa and addressed to Val d'Or should not be delivered the same day, when the distance between Ottawa and Val d'Or is covered in five hours, and between Montreal and Val d'Or, in seven or even six hours. In my opinion, there is no reason whatsoever for a letter mailed in the morning not to be delivered in Val d'Or the next morning.
Therefore, I urge the minister to ask his responsible officials in the postal service to inquire carefully into the delivery service provided to Val d'Or at present.
Mr. Chairman, those are the few remarks 1 wanted to make, and before resuming my seat, I repeat what I said at the beginning. I find the Postmaster General very understanding and co-operative with members of the house. Besides, he proved it by putting an end to political partisanship in order to provide efficient service to the population as a whole.
Is he bilingual?
In addition, Mr. Chairman, he is bilingual.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is in my capacity as member for Saint-Maurice-La-fleche that I wish to say a few words about the estimates of the Post Office Department.
I must say first that X am pleased to join with the member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), which is a rare occurrence. I also wish to congratulate the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) on the manner in which he performs his duties and, as the member for Villeneuve so rightly said, he is an understanding man.
I should like, therefore, to call his attention to a problem and ask his help on behalf of Shawinigan South a municipality of 15,000 .inhabitants, in the riding of Saint-Mau-rice-Lafleche.
Supply-Post Office
The good people of Shawinigan South do not have adequate mail service for their operations. There are a few post offices in grocery stores, but what is really needed for the numerous businessmen of Shawinigan South and the rest of the population, is a building where essential postal services would be provided, specially post office boxes, an adequate parcel post service open during lunch hour. In fact, several complaints have come to me from voters in Shawinigan South who cannot obtain proper service during lunch hour, because the two or three small post offices located in grocery or drug stores are not giving adequate service during lunch hour and, many times, people have to go to Shawinigan proper, that is three miles from Shawinigan South, to get normal postal service.
Many times in past years, I have made representations on this matter without results. That is why I am raising the question in the house today, because postal service is most important for the citizens of Shawinigan South. In fact, to obtain proper postal service, they have to cross the Shawinigan bridge, the two bridges on the St. Maurice river and finally get to the city of Shawinigan. I feel these people are entitled to adequate postal service, and this could be achieved by opening a sub-office in Shawinigan South. True, there is one already in the northern section, in St. Mark parish, but I suggest that the Postmaster General should ask for the necessary funds to establish a sub-office in the city of Shawinigan South, where the people have already made representations to that effect.
Once again, I congratulate the Postmaster General and and I urge him to keep up the good work in his job.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the members of this committee would like to hear from the Minister of Industry exactly what his department has done and what it intends to do under the estimates provided for the department at this time. I refer particularly, of course, to industry. Is industry in fact using the minister's department to the extent that would warrant these expenditures and the organization of this department? Is industry using it to a greater extent than the branch that existed for many years in the Department of Trade and Commerce? It is obvious that there has been a tremendous expansion in the Department of Industry and in its personnel compared with the facilities previously existing.
What puzzles me or raises some doubt in my mind is whether the activities of the department justify the expenditures involved here. I have talked to people in industry. They do not seem to know exactly how this department can help them. They want to know if the department is prepared to act in a consultative capacity? Is it there to give advice? If so, on what basis and in what

areas? As I understand it, the branch formerly existing under the Department of Trade and Commerce was set up for such purposes and was able to give industry much advice. I should like the minister to go into some detail to give us some idea about the points I have raised so as to clear the air and do away with the doubts existing in the minds of many people in industry regarding this department.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, although it has been some time since I have made a formal statement in the house on the operations of the Department of Industry I have the impression from the large number of questions I receive, both in the house and through correspondence, that members keep in close touch with the department's activities. I find this gratifying. The work we are doing is, I think, important to promoting this country's economic development and therefore of direct interest to all Canadians.
The formulation of a sound philosophy of operation deserves top priority in establishing any new department or agency of government. Some of the questions that have been put to me in the house and elsewhere indicate a very live interest in how we are going about the tasks which parliament has entrusted to the Department of Industry.
The department was established in recognition of the pressing need for Canada to attain an efficient expansion of our manufacturing industries. This is widely recognized as a necessary condition of sound economic growth, adequate employment opportunities for our rapidly growing labour force and an increase in our standard of living. It is not sufficient merely to expand our industries.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: May I interrupt the minister to ask him a question? Does that also include the rapid rise in the cost of living? Is that question also of importance to this department?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, one of the functions of the department is to increase productivity in Canada. With his knowledge of economics the hon. member for Ontario will recognize that this is one of the most effective ways of controlling undue rises in the cost of living.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: How is it being done? Could the minister explain that?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman would let me proceed, perhaps I could answer his question.
May 20, 1966

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I hope the minister will answer it.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
The hon. member asked a question and I proceeded to answer it. Before I had full opportunity to answer he asked another question. As I say, it is not merely sufficient to enlarge our industries or cause industries to grow. We must at the same time ensure that industrial efficiency improves. This of course means that we must place a high premium on improving productivity which is defined as output per man. Indeed, increased output per man is the only basis for improving our competitive position and for ensuring an increasing standard of living. To the extent that we achieve an improvement in productivity we will also be able to achieve our other economic goals such as stable prices and a viable balance of payments.
Government action can have a significant influence on the efficiency and rate at which the secondary manufacturing sector of the economy develops. The aim of the Department of Industry is to ensure that this influence is positive and helpful.
There are, of course, many factors which influence productivity. These include the quantity and quality of technology applied in industry, the level of education and skills of the labour force, the competence and imagination of our managers and entrepreneurs, the availability of capital, the environment of laws and regulations established by government, and the conditions governing access to foreign markets. The influence exerted by each of these factors on the growth of productivity varies between one sector of industry and another. The estimates now before you reflect a variety of programs to meet some of the more pressing problems of industrial development in Canada. Additional programs are being formulated and these will be proposed for your consideration during the coming year.
I should like to say a few words about the range of activities in which the department is engaged. First, we are developing a series of programs which will be helpful to industry generally in achieving efficient expansion. These include our activities to stimulate technological advance and improvement in our industrial design capability. Second, we have introduced a number of special programs to assist in solving problems unique to specific industry sectors. Examples are the automotive program, assistance to shipbuilding and our efforts to help the furniture industry.
Supply-Industry
Third, the department tries to ensure that policies and programs which are the responsibility of other federal government departments and agencies are formulated so as to provide industry with optimum opportunities for efficient expansion.
These activities can only be carried out effectively if the department attains a detailed and comprehensive knowledge of industry problems and devises good solutions, and if parliament votes the funds necessary to implement them. The task of obtaining a solid base of knowledge occupied a high proportion of our time during the first year or two of operations. This work has now been carried to a point where our efforts can be applied increasingly to the formulation and application of programs. This requires greater resources of money and manpower, and I think you can see this gradual shift in emphasis clearly reflected in the estimates.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
One of the major items of expenditure in departmental administration is the cost of wages and salaries. We are a small department in terms of numbers of personnel and we intend to keep it that way. At the same time, I think hon. members will agree that if we are to perform the tasks I have outlined we require an adequate number of highly qualified personnel to do the job.
A second major component of the administrative vote comprises a variety of expenditures related to information, communication and promotion. Industrialists who are aware of the latest developments in materials, equipment, managerial and production techniques, the changes in government regulations, and the market opportunities for their products, are in a better position to operate their businesses efficiently. No one can deny that good sound knowledge of what is going on in industry contributes significantly to effective entrepreneurial decisions, which are in turn a major determinant of business success.
Hon. members will see from our estimates that we attach a good deal of importance to providing the business community with current information on the opportunities available to them for improving their performance. This activity includes co-sponsoring research studies, the publication of reports on a wide range of technological, commercial, financial and market problems, and the sponsorship of technical missions, conferences and seminars; to increase knowledge of current practice within similar industries both at home and. in other countries.

May 20, 1966
Supply-Industry
The department is continuing its efforts to assist Canadian business in improving the design of Canadian products through a variety of education and information projects. Its programs include: scholarships and grants to provide financial assistance to students of industrial design for advanced study in Canada and abroad, and maintenance of the Canadian design index and the register of Canadian which provide data on products of Canadian designers, design and information to industry on designers and design services.
In order to ensure that Canadian businessmen may fully exploit the market opportunities generated by the centennial celebration and Expo '67, the department has undertaken to identify the types and volume of goods required to meet these needs and encourages Canadian businessmen to develop well designed Canadian made products to satisfy this demand. Concurrently, those concerned with planning and construction of centennial and Expo projects are made aware of the hundreds of products now available from Canadian sources which embody current concepts of industrial design.
The department maintains a design centre in Toronto to focus the attention of manufacturers, distributors, buyers and the general public on the need for well designed products. The department and the national design council will establish a second national design centre in Montreal in the near future. The department continues to co-operate with manufaturers' associations and professional groups in co-sponsoring a series of design award programs. Such programs have already been carried out in the field of structural steel and wood products. This year's schedule includes award programs to promote good design in electrical appliances and steel products.
While these projects involve an element of direct cost, their major cost impact is for the salaries and wages of personnel who plan and organize the projects. I believe that the results we have had to date from this activity justify the costs incurred. I am confident that our proposed expenditures for 1966-67 will be no less successful.
There are a number of major program items listed in the estimates. I would like to say a few words in explanation of each of these. In view of the fact that we only recently debated the resolution on the automotive agreement, I will not make specific reference to it here.

The area development program has sparked as much interest as any single program administered by my department. Hon. members are aware of the criteria used for designating areas eligible for development benefits and the scale of benefits provided. Accordingly, I would like to confine my comments to a review of the philosophy of the program. My earlier references to productivity were in terms of "output per man". There is another interpretation of the term which is more appropriate to apply in the case of area development. No nation can reach its full potential if it is suffering from high levels of unemployment. Not only do unemployed labour resources mean lost opportunities to increase output but they also involve welfare payments which constitute a further drain on resources that would otherwise be available for production purposes.
The federal government has, of course, a wide range of fiscal and other general measures designed to maintain a high level of national employment. Experience has shown, however, that some parts of the country do not respond adequately to those measures. They continue to suffer from higher levels of unemployment and lower levels of income than the rest of the country. The area development incentives are designed to encourage establishment of new industries or the expansion of existing industries in such areas, thereby supplementing federal full employment policies in a direct way and making them more effective. Since the program is designed to assist in that development of industrial employment opportunities in areas characterized by chronic unemployment and underemployment, the areas designated are those where unemployment is high, the rate of employment growth is low and income levels are well below the national level.
The degree of success achieved to date has been most encouraging. The department has received 450 firm notifications from companies that intend to establish or expand their facilities in designated areas. Our periodic program reviews have indicated that ten of the areas previously designated have reached levels of employment and income which put them outside the designation criteria. They were, therefore, removed from the list eligible for development benefits.
The results of the program are under continuing evaluation to help us refine the criteria for the definition of areas requiring assistance and also to help us formulate
May 20, 1966

supplementary programs which may be required to further our objective of bringing new economic opportunities to those parts of the country most in need of them.
The 1966-67 estimates provide funding for two programs aimed at encouraging increased research and development activity in Canadian industry. Until fairly recently Canada has relied very heavily on imported technology as a stimulus to industrial growth. For a country in its early stage of industrial development, reliance on imported technology is both necessary and desirable. I am sure we will continue to draw heavily on technology from abroad for many years to come. However, in view of increased international competition that has occurred over the past decade, Canadian industry must now begin to carve out a niche for itself in a number of selected areas of technological development. We must do this not only to increase our exports of manufactured goods but also to ensure maintenance of our domestic markets in conditions of freer world trade so much in vogue today.
The newly established program for the advancement of industrial technology P.A.I.T., is designed to promote the application of scientific and technological advances to the development of new products or processes for the commercial market. Essentially P.A.I.T., is a form of development insurance for underwriting selected development projects which involve a significant technical advance and which offer good prospects for commercial exploitation.
The initiative for proposing development projects and the responsibility for their direction rests with industry. All relevant costs of the projects are shared equally by the government and the firm. In the event the project is successful and the results are put to commercial use, the firm is required to repay the government's contribution with interest. Kepayment may extend over a period up to ten years. However, if the project is unsuccessful payback is waived. Proprietary rights resulting from the development project are vested in the firm, which is, of course, expected to exploit the results of the project in Canada.
Since the inception of this program some 20 projects have been approved and several times that number are being processed. In view of industry's response so far, I am confident this program will continue to grow and that we will begin to obtain concrete results within the next year or two.

employment as for road construction, bridge construction, and this cannot solve permanent conditions.
Industry is the basis and essential factor for the development of our country, for the creation of an environment where our people will be in a position to earn a living adequately.
I find the estimates are too high compared to the expenditures foreseen, because $20 million are provided for and this amount, as shown in the estimates, is made up entirely of grants. Nobody has to work to obtain a grant. Various amounts are shown but on what basis are those people paid for research?
Such is the situation, Mr. Chairman. I think the government should review the organization of these departments, entrust the ministers with responsibilities and draw up proper
budgets.
I sincerely believe that not only in the province of Quebec, but in every Canadian province from coast to coast, it would be possible by taking the trouble to maintain industries already established, to extend, modernize and develop them and even set up new industries. But it is not enough to say, as was announced yesterday on television: a new $50 million project in the province of Quebec, close to Ottawa. A few minutes later, somebody asked how many jobs would be provided. Seventy five more workers will get a job. A $50 million grant will be obtained, mind you, to create 75 jobs. Do you find this reasonable?
I am in favour of technocrats, economists and scientists, but departments need more than that. They actually need young men who know what constitutes an industry. We were told that a new industry would be established in Becancour at a cost of $300 to $700 million. We are now being told that the project is not believed to be workable. Such things give rise to a painful situation. The Minister of Labour is here today-and I am happy to congratulate him on his efforts-but he will realize that a problem has been created for him.
Because of the promises made to them, the farmers sold their farms or gave options on them. They no longer have the right to farm. For the last two years, they have been getting no income from their farms. As a matter of fact, they are running through their capital. They were promised a job and they are told now that no new industries will be established before five or six years to provide

May 20. 1966
Supply-Industry
them with jobs. They will be destitute, completely ruined and will become unemployed. Such is the present situation, and that is why I say the Minister of Industry has responsibilities.
Such a statement must not be made. We must not create such a situation.
In Montreal, soon, Expo '67 will take place. I tried to convince the minister yesterday that it was not necessary to carry out extensive work in St. Johns. We already have an airport there. All we need is to take immediate steps to modernize it. The municipality of St. Johns is ready to put up half a million dollars for the buildings. It would only cost the federal government $200,000 or $300,000 to expropriate the required properties. Do you know what he answered? My estimates do not provide for such work this year; we shall consider it next year. Well next year Expo '67 will be over and there will be no need for it. Action is needed right away. They just refuse to understand.
But for the province of Quebec, for my area, what matters most at this point, I am sure, is not so much giving money to industries as telling them: Here are the facilities, the reserves, income tax exemptions for two or three years, provided you increase your staff.
When a company tells the Department of Industry: Tomorrow morning, we are hiring 50 new employees; and another says: Tomorrow, we will take on 100 new employees. Then the government would be justified, with the co-operation of the Department of National Revenue and the Department of Industry in telling them: very well, we will give you a 10, 15 or 20 per cent exemption, according to the importance of the industry and the importance it is going to have.
It was not my intention to criticize the minister; compared to the other departments in Ottawa, his is a new one. But it is an important, a most important one. Let it have responsibilities and a budget; let the minister have enough power, I consider him competent in the industrial area and let him have employees, technicians and I suggest that the minister enlist businessmen in addition to economists and researchers.
Then, a plan could be drawn up to be applied, not in 20 years but this year, and next year, for such a program, I hope we can see something more in the budget than what there is now. It would not be a department concerned only with handing out

grants, but a department that will be creating jobs, careers, and which will bring relief to industry. Taxes now paralysing the development of existing industries are preventing new industries from getting started here and are a nuisance to small industries to the point where many will fail, because they will have to pay 1.8 per cent or half the contribution under the Canada pension plan.
There are small industries which are barely operating, so much so that the boss hardly earns a living wage. You realize there that you have been creating an impossible situation. Obviously nothing can be done about laws of a general nature and applicable to every one, but we should see to it that such industries do not fold up.
For ten years, while I was minister in Quebec, I was criticized, but we applied a policy of "visits and subsidies" to small industry with less than 100 employees. And do you know that in ten years there has not been a single bankruptcy among the industries we have helped. Some of them have developed since; others have expanded considerably, and one of the industries with which I was associated for 15 years was recently sold for $3,200,000, only because the owner died. Sixteen years ago this man could not borrow $25,000 from the bank. Why was he so successful? Because he was helped, because the department helped him.
I ask the minister this. His department needs not only technicians and research workers, but auditors and engineers who should give industry across Canada the information it requests free of charge. This would be a most essential service. These people would be paid by the Ottawa government and their services would be available to whoever needs them.
There are research centres in large industries which can afford to hire engineers. When a company pays $5 million for research, it does not need help. On the other hand, small business concerns which today operate on a marginal basis need an engineer or a chartered accountant to do research. These concerns should be helped.
Why should the government not make available to these people, at its own expense, qualified men who would submit a report. This would not be unreasonably expensive. In two months a good engineer can tell you if a small industry is economically sound, if it should be maintained or closed.
Auditors will look into a business concern, study production costs and tell the people:
May 20, 1966

Gentlemen, you are selling below cost, you cannot succeed. Your concern is not competitive. I believe this is a practical policy and that the minister, who is a business man, realizes that if he could set up such a system he would do the provinces and the whole country a great service, including his colleagues heading such departments as labour, trade and commerce, finance and revenue.
We can have a prosperous Canada. We can have prosperous provinces, on one condition: that we organize ourselves scientifically, seriously, and that we put competent people in all the departments and divisions.
[DOT] (2:00 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, I want to make a few brief remarks on the minister's estimates as an unrepentant old socialist trying to look at these questions from a fundamental and traditional socialist point of view.
I see the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration looking at me over the top of his glasses. I hope we will assist him in the programs he has undertaken to date by what we say this afternoon and will say later.
I suppose it is correct to say that the Department of Industry is the department of wait and see. That is the general attitude of most hon. members. The department has to prove itself, but I am sure all members of this group wish the minister and his officials every success in all they undertake to try to fill the gaps that have been left in employment, development, markets and research as a result of the monopoly control of our economy by a few large industrial giants.
The minister knows that we in this party are traditionally opposed to monopoly and combine. We have had that plank in our program since our movement was first formed in 1932. We have maintained that position and intend to maintain it. There are two major groups that actually control the Canadian economy. One is the small but powerful Canadian economic elite described by various persons as all those who are involved in Canadian owned corporations which have interlocking directorships. The other is a group of United States firms and foreign businesses which have a tremendous influence on social and economic conditions in Canada.
I am not blaming individuals. These persons have their functions to perform in the society in which we live and they have their
Supply-Industry
duties as directors and officers of corporations. As I say, I am not blaming individuals.
I am just bringing to the minister's attention some of the highlights of our program in case he might want to fall back on them in the months ahead.
I wish to quote from "Notes For Speakers 1965" provided to the New Democratic Party, and I hope the minister will read the booklet later. There is a section headed "How Do The Giant Firms Keep Their Supremacy" which reads:
Someone may well wonder how the dominant corporations in each industry manage to stay on top. In view of the fact that they earn large profits, why doesn't this attract so many new firms into the industry that the share of the dominant firms is sharply reduced?
That is a good question.
There are a number of ways in which the giants can bar or discourage new firms from entering the industry.
1.	In some industries enormous amounts of capital are required to establish a new plant and only the existing dominant firms have this kind of capital.
2.	Some industries require a particular natural resource or type of skill and the available supply of these may be completely controlled by the existing firms. Sometimes this takes the form of "vertical integration" where the large firm controls everything from the raw material supplies to the marketing of the end products.
3.	Often the existing firm secures a patent on a particular process or product which bars new firms from using this process or producing this product.
I am sure the minister and his officials have had some experience in that regard in looking at Canadian industry as it is today.
4.	The large existing firms have well established sources of credit to supply them with funds for expansion. Credit is not so readily available to the small firm. The large firms can also float huge issues of stocks and bonds; this is very difficult indeed for a new firm just beginning operations.
I understand the minister's department intends to promote the issuance of credit to sound industries being promoted on a large and small scale.
5.	The most successful advertising is that which is carried out on a national scale-on television and radio, in national magazines, etc. The large existing firms can afford this; newcomers generally cannot.
I am quite sure the great majority of small industries and businesses could not undertake this sort of advertising on any scale.
6.	The dominant firms have surplus funds with which to carry out costly research into new methods and products.
7.	The large corporation can engage the newcomer in a price war. The giant has reserves which will sustain him until the war is over;-

May 20, 1966
Supply-Industry
I have seen that happen in the retail business in my own district.
-the newcomer generally does not have such reserves and is driven out ol the market. Then the giant restores the price to its former level.
These are only a few of the methods by which the existing dominant corporations maintain their hold on an industry.
How do many of these people acquire their capital? The minister has talked about incentives to promote industry in certain areas. We have provided massive incentives for these monopolies whether they are Canadian owned or United States owned.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
I have an article I cut from the Ottawa Journal of May 18. I will read briefly from it because the figures are handy, Possibly I could have located the figures had I searched my files. This is a report of a speech made in the legislature of Ontario by Mr. Kenneth Bryden. He had this to say:

the plain fact is that "only a very small and declining amount of U.S. investment funds," is associated with U.S. corporate control in Canada.
The went on to illustrate his statement that Americans are buying us out with our own money. He said:
-in 1964 about $764,000,000, or 40 per cent of the total net U.S. financing in Canada, came from the depreciation and depletion reserves of Canadian subsidiaries of U.S. corporations.
The report continues:
He said an additional $644,000,000 came from undistributed profits of these subsidiaries and the remaining $423,000,000 came from stocks and bonds sold outside the U.S.
He said U.S. corporations "are re-investing funds generated in Canada which they have captured in depreciation allowances and undistributed funds."
As a solution to U.S. control Mr. Bryden suggested reform of provincial and federal corporation tax structures to tighten up provisions regarding depreciation and depletion allowances.
This really is a massive form of tax incentive which has provided a great deal of the capital throughout the years for United States controlled subsidiaries in Canada. I wish to draw this to the particular attention of the minister because it seems to me there should be some consideration of the larger investment in Canada of capital obtained in this way.
Before concluding I should like to offer to the minister a few suggestions from our New Democratic Party program. This is the present program; you can rely on it. If the minister would like to have one of these booklets I would be glad to send on over to

him later. What would happen, Mr. Chairman, if we should over the months ahead get a convert? We will do our best to see that he has the information.

Mr. Chairman, if I may have the indulgence of the committee and the minister for a few moifients I should like to pick up where my colleague the hon. member for Halifax left off on the question of the area incentive program. The minister has heard the blessings which have been expressed in respect of this piece of legislation. As the hon. member for Halifax has mentioned, the minister received communications in the form of letters, briefs, and so on from the mayors of the four distinct areas of Halifax, Dartmouth, Saint John, Fredericton and the municipalities or areas immediately surrounding these cities. Latterly he has heard collectively from the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council which represents, as has been suggested, a non-political group. This should carry added weight in reassuring the government of the necessity of moving in some concerted manner to overcome the regional disparities which exist in the Atlantic provinces.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
It has been suggested that unemployment figures are the criterion for the area incentive program in the regions in which it is applicable. It is not necessary for me to recite the employment and unemployment figures in British Columbia, the prairie region, Ontario, Quebec and in our region, the maritimes. I think hon. members are very familiar with them. Therefore, suffice it that I draw to your attention one or two facts. On March 19 this year, according to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, employment stood at 6.821 million and unemployment at 341,000, which means
Supply-Industry
that somewhere in the order of 5 per cent of our national labour force was out of work on that date. In the maritime provinces on March 19 there were 537,000 people at work. On the same date there were 63,000 people out of work. The relationship between these figures is very obvious. In our area 63,000 people out of work represent approximately 12 per cent of our total labour force whereas the national average was only in the order of 5 per cent. I will not draw the more startling comparisons that are obvious in respect of the Ontario, prairie and British Columbia regions.
The necessity of dealing with the problems of industrial development and productivity in the Atlantic region has been brought so forcibly to the attention of the government, civic leaders, economists and everybody concerned that there is very little I can do except reiterate what appears to be a mounting volume of evidence to support two or three very basic propositions. The first of these is the need to approach the problems of the Atlantic region in the spirit that has been voiced so often by the government, the spirit of equal opportunity and equal sharing in our national prosperity. This is not easy to achieve, as pointed out by the Economic Council of Canada and by APEC. Any economist who has studied the relationship of the Maritimes to the rest of Canada has come to the same conclusion in one way or another, and that conclusion is simply that the problems cannot be approached piecemeal but rather must be attacked by one concerted effort.
The minister is very much aware of this but in spite of the pleas and urgings to pursue this course the government has not yet seen fit to do so. We do have the Atlantic provinces development board and the area incentive program, but I suggest to the minister that if he cannot modify, extend or enlarge the regulations under these programs at once to embrace the four areas mentioned, Saint John, Dartmouth, Halifax and Fredericton, which are the growth centres of the Atlantic region and are now outside any special incentive program, the help needed will not be forthcoming.
Because these are the growth centres and the centres to which people from rural areas will be attracted, a great percentage of whom are unemployed, the government must give serious consideration to them. It has been suggested that it is of no avail to locate an industry in a region, district or area where

May 20, 1966
Supply-Industry
there are not the labour, goods, materials, processes and markets to support it. It has been suggested that experience may well prove that many of these companies located in so-called designated areas are going to remain burdens on the economy for a long time to come simply because they have been misplaced, whereas if they had been placed in growth centres as they have wanted to be traditionally this would have created stability in the over-all area rather than instability. Urban people will not go to rural areas to work but rural people will come into urban areas.
To illustrate further the effect of what is happening in the Atlantic area I should like to point out to hon. members that in 1960, for example, per capita production in the Atlantic provinces stood at $218. The national average in Canada at the same time was very nearly $600-$589 to be exact. That is more than double and it indicates there is something seriously wrong. It also indicates that with government help through a concerted program on the part of the minister we will arrive at a situation where we can bring in new industry, promote stability and broaden the economic base. This will bring about diversification and will create incentives for other industries to expand.
If we are to survive as members of the whole, and I speak of members of Canada as a nation, the Atlantic provinces area must find 20,000 new jobs each year for the next few years. At the end of five years this figure will be closer to 30,000 and, indeed, I hope it will be closer to 40,000. But without some concerted form of over-all approach to the problems of the Atlantic region we are not even going to be able to provide the 20,000 new jobs that will have to be created there. I do not think the necessary approach is an area incentive program but rather a broader based area approach must be taken to solve this problem.
The figure of 20,000 jobs means that we will simply maintain our present growth rate. There are any number of standards by which to measure this. While we are going ahead we are not keeping pace with the gross national product For example, in 1947 Nova Scotia-I single our Nova Scotia because this area is perhaps illustrative of Atlantic region problems-enjoyed, to our dismay, per capita incomes that only reached about 81 per cent of the national average. That was less than 20 years ago. While incomes in 1964 had risen in terms of total dollars, it is significant to note 
that in comparison with 81 per cent of the national average figure in 1947 we enjoyed only 74.8 per cent. This is indicative of what is happening in the Atlantic region. The failure on the part of the government to approach the problems of the Atlantic region on a broad basis has created this situation. It has been created in spite of our own efforts to keep up by helping to create that atmosphere in which our economic growth could at least keep pace with the national growth.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
I have some other figures that are illustrative of what is happening. In 1961 we had 3.65 million families in Canada. Of these families 77 per cent enjoyed, and undoubtedly do now to an even greater degree, annual incomes in excess of $3,000 per year. Taking the figures for the Atlantic provinces, of
86.000	families in Newfoundland 49 per cent, have incomes in excess of $3,000. The national average is 77 per cent. In Prince Edward Island, our smallest province, 55 per cent of the 14,000 families receive $3,000 or more. In the province of Nova Scotia where we have
147.000	families and, thank God, an excellent premier, the figure is 63 per cent. This is still 14 per cent below the national average. In New Brunswick where there are 111,000 families only 61 per cent earn $3,000 or more. Every other province in Canada has at least 68 per cent or more of its families in the $3,000 plus bracket. If one removes the figures for the Atlantic provinces from the national average one finds that 82 per cent of the families of Canada enjoy annual incomes in excess of $3,000.
The same pattern emerges when one considers per capita income. In Ontario the figure is $2,025. In Newfoundland it is $1,009. Listing the provinces in the order in which they stand in the income per capita field we find Ontario leading the way-there is no doubt about that-with British Columbia second, Alberta third, Saskatchewan next_
Good old Saskatchewan.
"Good old Saskatchewan"-I would remind the hon. member that had it not been for the Atlantic provinces there would be no Saskatchewan.
We are out of the have-not area.

You are. We are still in it. In Saskatchewan the income per capita amounts to $1,749. In my own province of
May 20, 1966

Nova Scotia it is $1,302; in New Brunswick it is $1,167 and in Prince Edward Island, $1,115.
Reciting these figures takes the time of the committee but I simply wish to substantiate the point I am making, that in the absence of an over-all approach to the problems of the Atlantic region we shall never achieve any degree of national parity, any reasonable share in the wealth of this nation.
The vehicles which the federal government can use in its approach to the problems of the Atlantic area are already in existence. There is no need to set up another crown corporation or establish a ministry for the Atlantic region. Industrialization can take place through existing arrangements. I ask the minister whether he is completely confident that nothing can be done to change the area incentive regulations so as to include the principle of growth centres such as Halifax, Dartmouth, Saint John and Fredericton. If this is impossible in terms of other criteria which have been set up I would ask the minister to urge his colleagues to give consideration to the broadening of the base upon which the Atlantic Development Board operates. I urge him to ask his colleagues to consider broadening the scope of its regulations so as to permit the board to make direct capital grants to industry as well as to make settling-in grants for a period up to three years. I suggest that the Atlantic Development Board remains the one real hope among the existing vehicles. There are others which could be overlooked despite their importance. I shall not on this occasion discuss the fields of research and technical development.
What we in the Atlantic provinces need is the industry so that we could do some research for ourselves. We have to get the industry first. While a good job is being done within the present framework of the Atlantic Development Board, this is not enough. There has to be an over-all effort aimed at every area of endeavour, not just those areas which endeavour to supply the service element, by which I mean the development of industrial parks, water and sewage services and so on. These are very necessary and I would be the last to suggest that what the development board has done has not been excellently done and of great value. But it does not go far enough.
Unless we take a fresh look at this situation we are bound to see a repetition of what has been happening in Halifax during the last 12 to 14 months. There is a real possibility of losing a $60 million fisheries based industry.
Supply

Industry
We have already lost a chemical industry based on oil refining. We nearly lost Volvo, Canada, which was brought to this country after great effort involving co-operation between the provincial and the federal governments. It was only by a special effort on the part of the provincial authority that we managed to keep it in Nova Scotia at all.
Many other opportunities have been lost or nearly lost to this area because we are outside the range of special tax incentives. Again I would ask the minister to take a hard look at the whole basis of the regulations governing the Atlantic Development Board should he consider it impossible to revise the criteria applying to the designated areas.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a few words only on the first item of these estimates. At the outset I should like to tell the Minister of Industry that I realize there has been a certain amount of criticism, some of it valid and some of it possibly not so valid, directed toward the activities of this new department. There have no doubt been problems in recruiting a suitable staff and settling in. This may have prevented the department from taking all the action it might have taken to promote the development of industry in Canada. I also want the minister to know that we in this party give him full support for whatever programs and undertakings his department can initiate to promote and enhance our industrial establishments in Canada.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I think we should direct the attention of the minister to some of the provisions of the designated area program, and perhaps for different reasons than those which have been advanced in the house so far today. I say this because I feel we need to be concerned about the long-range effect of the establishment of industries in these designated areas. I believe that in the course of time it will be shown that some misplaced industries have been set up in these areas because of the incentives available for establishment there. There will be problems, I suggest, for those industries if they are to continue to be competitive with other industries producing the same class of goods and which may be more efficient because of their proximity to raw materials and markets.
I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that it is a great burden for any municipality to have an

May 20, 1966
Supply-Industry
industry which cannot meet the kind of competition it will face in the ordinary course of business after the benefits of the original incentives have lapsed. I suggest we also have a responsibility in the federal administration to see that those economic areas which are strong today remain so. In this way they will be able to assist some of the so-called depressed areas over this period. The only plea I make is that we do not go too far with the designated area program so that we weaken some of the stronger areas and then find ourselves with a lot of misplaced industries. This certainly would undermine our whole economic establishment, particularly when we must be competitive in the international field.
While talking about designated areas, Mr. Chairman, may I say there are some factors involved in the formula establishing designated areas which should be examined. I am not suggesting now that anyone ought to have anticipated all the problems that may arise from time to time. However, it does seem to me that the various factors involved in whether or not an area is going to be designated should be under continuous review. One thing that has shown up is that the level of unemployment in an area seems to be far too heavily weighted at the present time. I say that because in certain communities in southern Alberta, for example, there has been an exodus of unemployed from these areas to places where there are employment opportunities; yet the growth and income level factors meet the requirements for a designated area within the program. I suggest that this is going to encourage, as some members have said, a further concentration of industry in the larger urban areas. Personally I believe that this is not desirable over the long range.
I should like now to deal with another matter affecting southern Alberta. In Medicine Hat constituency an industry was established not very long ago for the processing of potatoes. It ran into some problems in connection with a processing patent. I would have thought this would be a problem in which the Department of Industry would be keenly interested and actively involved in trying to solve it. Without attempting to be unduly critical, I do not believe that the representations made by the industry and the provincial government received the kind of response they should have received from the Department of Industry.

There was, for example, some patent litigation over the processing method that had been developed by a branch of the federal government. It seemed to me that these people were left to their own resources to fight these legal problems. On balance, I think if justice were to be done the federal government, particularly the Department of Industry, should have assumed some responsibility with regard to the litigation.
I say that, Mr. Chairman, because this was a good industry. The equipment appeared to be modern and of excellent design. It was located in an area where the potential for the raw material, potatoes, was great. It seemed to me that everything was there. The location was ideal and the industry would have been beneficial not only to the farmers in the area but to the investors in the industry and to Canada. However, it collapsed. It is still not running because while the legal battle is over the delay and the clouded issue hanging over the whole project for so many months have made it difficult to resume operations.
I do not want to be unduly critical of the minister and his department because the department was in the formative stages at the time. However, it seems to me that the federal government should go to the aid of an industry in such a situation because certainly the people who tried to get it going and invested their money could not be blamed for it. I hope arrangements have now been made so that the plant can get into production. I do not know whether that is the case but certainly there has been no activity around the plant yet.
I have referred to this plant as an example of something with which I feel the Department of Industry could have been concerned. I hope that in the future they will be more actively interested in problems of this kind.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, I intend to be brief but it seems to me that because of a lack of action on the part of several departments, not only the Department of Industry, it has become necessary for provincial governments to make direct contact with certain foreign countries to try to promote industrial growth. I am not suggesting that this is wrong, but I suggest that the reason provincial government representatives have had to take this step is that not enough initiative is being taken by the federal government.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
For example, British Columbia only a short time ago sent a trade mission to Japan not only for the purpose of promoting trade but
May 20, 1966

also for the purpose of promoting additional industrial establishment in British Columbia. The premier of Alberta is in Japan at the present time and I presume, although I do not know for sure, that discussions will be held there with a view to expanding certain primary industries in Alberta which will be beneficial both to that province and to Japan. Newfoundland has had direct discussions with industrialists in the United Kingdom and Europe.
In matters such as this it should be the prime responsibility of the federal government to carry on negotiations and discussions with foreign countries. Therefore I hope that in the future the Department of Industry will become more active in assisting industries already established in Canada such as the one I have mentioned, and will also do some of the work which the provinces seem to have taken on and which I believe is perhaps a little out of their field, particularly when they are having discussions and conducting negotiations with representatives of foreign countries.
